blocks.x: It's a natural thing for some people.

Do you find like there's a- Of course you have to give something too, you know what I mean. You have to give a performance. Like I try to, when I always did any band I worked with, I tried to sell the band. I tried to do my best to put it over. I give all I can and that's all you can do. If you like it, okay. You know what?
There's not much you can do.

There's one of the things that I do. See like that picture over there? That's what I get out there and do. Have you found- I guess you've seen all that because I guess you've come around, you've been around Jap because he wants to have stuff like that too. See all of that stuff they gave me over there?
Uh huh. Yeah. Mainly I notice all the posters up on the wall. Yeah.
We've got letters all back then.
Have you found like in the past fifteen years that jazz is being appreciated, like a lot more people are listening to?

Well yeah. What would happen, I think the jazz club had a whole lot to do with keeping it alive. Because I used to do a whole lot of it. I don't know if you know, Harry Schuchon and Doc Schuchon. They're French. Well there was Helen Ault and all of them. I don't know if you know her. You don't know anything about jazz at all then. You don't know them because they don't want to keep the jazz club. Still it's not as live as it should be now. But they kept it and we used to, our group, used to do a lot of gratties for them. We'd play their concerts and things you know. It was free. They'd get places at the hotels and buy drinks and stuff like that. They didn't make any money. And once in a while now they give concerts now. But I think by the jazz club that kept the things sort of alive and they'd get their people to give their services, musicians. And I really believe that sort of helped them. Well they have a whole lot of jazz clubs all open now. And I'm an honorary member to two or three of them. I was a financial member here but I didn't pay my dues last year.
Where do you like to play the most? Which city? New Orleans? Well I don't know.
I'd rather be home I think. If I could make the money that I get on the road here I'd prefer staying here.
But you can't.

You can just get the union skills. Of course the Japanese is very nice. He plays a little better in the union skills. I don't think I'd want to work every night at this age. I think I could live without it. Not as well as you and your dad and your mama. Because you're not mine, huh? No. But you ain't got nothing to worry about. Not yet? No. You've got a nice mother, nice daddy. How old are you? Twenty-five.
How do you find being on the road now different than say when you were working on the ...

Well it's a whole lot different. Like in what way? It's a whole lot different in many ways. Like in what way? It's more expensive, but you get, it's convenient, it's much more pleasant than before. Like traveling especially with the Japanese jurisdiction where he's been handling, he's been treating the musicians very nice. So I've traveled on the roads before, I've worked with Miller and I wasn't getting a whole lot of money. But everybody had to hand out like Henry Clay. We had a valet who used to travel with us. He was getting a salary. But anytime you ask him to do something, one of them would figure, I used to play a theater listen, he'd have to do something, he'd expect him something. Like he'd want a sandwich or he'd want your clothes pressed, your shoes shined, things like that. And what you're going to do is $75 a week. Of course they paid the transportation, but you paid your own hotel bill. It was expensive then according to the times. Of course now it's more expensive because you go to one of the hotels and you run anywhere from $35 to $40 a night. And that's a whole lot of expense. And I don't like that. That's the part I really don't like. When we started out it was very nice and you could get a place for $12, $15, you know, sometimes $9 or $10 and they had some places, they advertised they'd spare $6. You get that in the moment. It was very nice, I enjoyed it. In fact I like playing music. I've done a whole lot for nothing so now I'm able to get a little money. I've been doing a lot.
Do you think you'll keep on traveling a lot?
As long as I'm able to walk I guess, I think they'll still want me. They could do without me though I guess, you know, for a dime. Yeah. Yeah.
Um, when you were traveling on the, traveling around Mainland 30s, were there a lot of traveling
bands at that time?
You said there were two boats and four bands. But you know.

Well the two biggest bands that I remember, or not the two bands, I had a whole lot of bands that traveled but they were big bands you see. But we had regular work. But these other jobs they had one-nighters like Fletcher Henderson, McKinney's Cotton Pickers. They were the first bands that I can remember during the time, that they got a thousand dollars a night. That was a whole lot of money for a band. Way back there. Well I think they had a band they called Gene Goldkatt out of Detroit, that's where this band McKinney is. And I think they were booking them out there. So Gene Goldkatt had a whole lot of bands under their name, like the Preservation Hall. See they had two or three bands and that's what they did. Gene Goldkatt had bands different places. Yeah they had a whole lot of bands. They had a whole lot of bands come out of Florida. They had a hell of a band. They had a whole lot of bands on the radio. Al Ponce O' Trent come out of Texas, and a hell of a band. Second to none of the bands. That's second to Duke Allington and none of the rest of them. Duke Allington was on the road. That's another, Duke Allington was tops at the time you see. But they had other bands. I had occasion to listen to the three top bands at that time. That was McKinney's Cotton Pickers, Duke Allington, and Fletcher Henderson on the one road. It was great. Then you had Noble Sisterly had a band on the road. They had a whole lot of bands on the road. Larry James had a big band, as many of them. Glenn Miller, they had a whole lot of bands out on the road. Some of them did one-nighters and some of them did out of the Goldwick.
But most of the bands on the road at that time were the big bands, not the ...

Well I guess they had smaller bands but the big bands had the names there. Well they could afford to pay them. Now it's kind of hard to pay a big band because the price is well. What they do, they still have them, was Basie now, you take the band that Basie's got. It was called Kansas City or something, see? And that was a big band. Basie was a piano player and they said he took the band over. Well they had a whole lot of big bands on the road. I just can't remember all the names, you know. And they were all good.
They had a big band.

They had a big band. They used to be on the road right out of here. They worked all in Florida, Alabama, Georgia, all around this area, all through Louisiana, Mississippi, and they had a lot of value. So a lot of fellas, I don't know what kind of money they made, but some of them I never would go nowhere with. I'd sooner stay home and just job around.
Let me check. . .

Yeah, I have a daughter, she finishes music education. She does a little substitute work. She's got eight children. One of them is sitting here with me, he goes to Xavier College. My youngest boy. My youngest boy.

segments.title: Selling the band and the memorabilia on the wall
segments.summary: Humphrey says he always tried to sell whatever band he worked with and gives his best; he points to pictures, posters and letters on the wall.

segments.title: The jazz clubs that kept jazz alive in New Orleans
segments.summary: He credits the local jazz clubs with keeping the music alive, recalling free concerts his group played for them and his honorary memberships.

segments.title: Preferring to stay home versus working on the road
segments.summary: He would rather stay in New Orleans if the money matched the road, and does not want to work every night at his age; the talk drifts to the interviewer's age.

segments.title: Touring today compared with the old road days
segments.summary: Road travel is now more expensive but more pleasant under a considerate tour manager; he recalls $75 a week, paying his own hotel, tipping a valet, and plans to keep traveling.

segments.title: Big touring bands of the 1930s: McKinney's, Henderson, Ellington
segments.summary: He recalls the big road bands of the 30s, naming McKinney's Cotton Pickers, Fletcher Henderson, Duke Ellington, Alphonso Trent and Noble Sissle, and Goldkette's booking.

segments.title: Big bands, Basie, and bands touring the Gulf South
segments.summary: Big bands had the names and could afford to pay; he mentions Basie and bands working Florida to Mississippi, saying he preferred staying home and jobbing around.

segments.title: His daughter and youngest son
segments.summary: After a break, he mentions his daughter, a music educator with eight children, and his youngest son at Xavier College.
